metadata.title: Before the Numbers
metadata.author: Amos Jaimes
metadata.note: Two strands from the weekly report: paper preparation, and a base-size rerun of model A. Neither new experiment has been run. Measured numbers on screen are prior results quoted from the report (plain CNN vs ResNet vs published; the size trial; last week's 0.23 miss). Everything about the rerun's outcome is a FORECAST or a pre-set RULE, and the narration says so. No code run, no fact-checking, by instruction.

beats.narration_text: Two jobs this week, and neither one produces a result yet. Write the paper up honestly, before the experiment that will fill it has run. And find out whether a bigger version of the pretrained model would have done better, without letting the answer be argued into a win afterwards.

props.command: Check my paper outline against the data and code we actually have. Then set up a rerun of the pretrained model at a larger size, and write down what would count as an improvement before anything runs.
output: Fix the decision rules first, then launch.

beats.narration_text: So: a paper outline that survived contact with the data, mostly. One part had to be redesigned and the core experiment still needs new code. And a larger model, fully configured, with nothing launched. The most likely outcome is small, and the rules for judging it are already written down.

props.text:
A paper, set up honestly.
A bigger model, not yet run.

The rules come first.

beats.narration_text: The paper compares plain one-dimensional CNNs with residual networks, on the bacteria data Ho and colleagues published in 2019. So far the evidence points the unexpected way. Our small plain CNN reaches eighty three point nine. Our ResNet, over six times its size, reaches seventy nine point six. Published: eighty two point two. So the paper asks whether residual connections matter, rather than assuming they win.

props.title: Plain CNN versus ResNet, so far
props.caption: Test accuracy percent, three seeds each, before any controlled comparison

beats.narration_text: One part did not survive. The outline planned to compare noise across one, two and three second exposures. The data has no such splits: the reference set is one second, and everything else is two seconds at about the same signal to noise. So that part becomes a simulated noise sweep, plus the real one to two second instrument shift that is already in the data.

lines: The data has no 1, 2 and 3 second splits.
Replaced by a simulated noise sweep,
plus the real 1 to 2 second instrument shift.
meta: no sample IDs either, so the original split protocol is kept

beats.narration_text: And the central comparison cannot run yet. Our current ResNet is not the published architecture, and it differs from our CNN in about seven ways at once. Any gap between them could come from any of those seven. Isolating the effect of skip connections needs a faithful port of the twenty five layer ResNet, a plain twin matched in depth and width, and then one change at a time.

lines: Our ResNet differs from our CNN in seven ways.
So skip connections cannot be isolated yet.
Next: a matched plain twin, one change at a time.

beats.narration_text: Now the second job. The pretrained model's size was chosen in a short trial. Small and base tied, so the smaller one was kept. Then a fix to the model's first layers lifted small from point six seven two to point seven four two. But that fix was only ever applied to small. Base, with the fix, has never been run. And last week's adapters missed their goal by under a quarter of a point. A bigger frozen model gives them more to steer.

props.title: Base was never tested with the fix
props.caption: Probe score after 50 epochs. Base with the fix: never run.

beats.narration_text: What to expect, as a forecast, not a result: most likely a small gain, zero to two points. Validation is already ninety five to ninety nine percent, test eighty three to ninety two. That gap comes from new cultures and a later clinical year, which a bigger encoder does not fix. Its best chances are the adapters and scarce labels. And fourteen million parameters on nine thousand clinical spectra may simply overfit.

lines: The limit is the shift, not the model size.
Best chances: adapters, and scarce labels.
meta: full fine-tuning may overfit 9,000 clinical spectra

beats.narration_text: And the rules, fixed before running. Adopt base only if its trial beats small by more than point zero three, the same tie rule as before. Compare each arm with the same paired tests, choosing on validation only. Scoring the test sets again is a second comparison, and it gets declared as one. And with one pretraining seed each, a gap under about a point may just be seed noise.

Your turn. Before you rerun anything bigger, write down what result would make you switch, and what would make you stay. Here is a prompt for that. The value is in answering it before you see the number, not after.

props.command: I am about to rerun my model at a larger size. Before I launch it, help me write the decision rules: what margin counts as a real improvement, which comparisons I am allowed to make, and how I will report it if the result is close.

beats.narration_text: Before the numbers. Working notes from a Humanitarians AI fellowship. The failures are the part worth keeping.
